config.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared

intro.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds all numbers missing from a given array of integers, where the array contains numbers from 1 to n but some may be missing. You will learn the core concept of using an array as a hash map to mark visited numbers efficiently. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays, loops, and conditional logic. This approach helps solve the problem without extra space, making it optimal for beginners to understand array manipulation and indexing.
intro.usecase: The 'Find All Numbers Disappeared' pattern is essential for data validation and integrity checks in real applications. For example, in inventory management dashboards, it can identify missing product IDs in a shipment sequence, ensuring complete tracking. In user analytics panels, it helps detect gaps in sequential user activity logs or missing timestamps in event streams. This algorithm also powers form validation by finding skipped entries in numbered form submissions or missing steps in multi-step workflows.

objectives: Implement a function that identifies missing numbers in a given array of integers
Apply a marking strategy to track visited numbers within the original array
Construct a result array to collect numbers not found during traversal
Manipulate array indices to mark elements without using extra space
Initialize and configure the algorithm to handle arrays with values from 1 to n
Integrate the marking and collection steps into a complete solution
Control the iteration process to traverse the array exactly once for marking and once for collection

content.body: Sometimes numbers go missing in an array, but we can find them with a clever trick. In this lesson, you'll learn how to efficiently discover which numbers disappeared from a sequence using a simple notebook approach.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
1. Apply a hash map to track seen numbers in an array.
2. Implement an algorithm to find all missing numbers in O(n) time.
3. Explain why checking a lookup structure is faster than scanning repeatedly.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Which numbers from 1 to 5 are missing in this array?
content.successMessage: Good! 4 is missing from the sequence 1-5.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Which numbers from 1 to 8 are missing here?
content.successMessage: Nice work! 5 and 6 are missing from 1-8.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Find missing numbers from 1 to 10 in this array.
content.successMessage: Excellent! You found 6 and 8 are missing. You likely checked each number 1-10 against the array.

content.body: You just performed a brute force check: for each number in the range, you scanned the array to see if it was present. This works for small arrays but becomes inefficient as arrays grow larger.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 100,000 numbers, scanning for each possible number becomes extremely slow. We need a smarter method that avoids repeated scanning. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of scanning repeatedly, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to note which numbers we've encountered, then check that structure in one step.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen. When we want to know if we've seen a number, we just check the notebook instead of searching through everything again.

content.body: We'll mark all numbers we see in a lookup structure, then check which numbers from 1 to n are missing.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Array: [4,3,2,7,8,2,3,1], n=8
1. Create empty notebook (object).
2. For each number in array: write it in notebook (seen[4]=true, seen[3]=true...).
3. Check numbers 1-8: if not in notebook, it's missing.
4. Missing: 5,6 (not in notebook).

content.body:
1. Create an empty object to act as our 'seen' notebook.
2. Loop through the input array: for each number, mark it as seen in the notebook.
3. Create a result array for missing numbers.
4. Loop from 1 to n (array length): if a number isn't in the notebook, add it to results.
5. Return the result array.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function skeleton
steps.instruction: Start by creating a function called findDisappearedNumbers that takes one parameter nums.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or arrow syntax.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function declaration with correct name and parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure the function name is exactly findDisappearedNumbers.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function that accepts nums as a parameter.

steps.title: Initialize the lookup structure
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create an empty object called seen. This will be our notebook to track which numbers we've encountered.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we have a place to remember what we've seen.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure you're creating an empty object with {}.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need an empty object to store seen numbers. Try const seen = {};

steps.title: Mark seen numbers in the notebook
steps.instruction: Loop through the nums array and mark each number as seen in your notebook object. Use for...of loop.
steps.hint: for (let num of nums) { seen[num] = true; }
steps.expectedOutcome: Loop that marks each number in seen object
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now our notebook records every number we encounter.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure you're assigning true to seen[num] inside the loop.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to iterate through nums and mark each number. Try a for...of loop.

steps.title: Check for missing numbers
steps.instruction: Create a result array and check numbers from 1 to nums.length. If a number isn't in the seen notebook, add it to results.
steps.hint: Use a for loop from 1 to nums.length, and check if (!seen[i]).
steps.expectedOutcome: Loop that finds missing numbers and adds to result array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! Now we're finding which numbers are missing by checking our notebook.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure you're checking if the number is NOT in seen before adding to results.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to check each number 1 through n. If it's not in seen, it's missing.

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: Finally, return the result array from your function.
steps.hint: Add return result; at the end of the function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your function now returns all missing numbers efficiently.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure you're returning the result array.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to return the result array so the function gives back the missing numbers.

content.body: Great work! You've implemented an efficient O(n) solution using a hash map approach. Remember: the key insight is to use a lookup structure to remember what we've seen, avoiding repeated scans. This 'notebook' pattern is powerful for many array problems where you need to track occurrences or check membership quickly.
content.title: Done
